blocks.p: Nouns are really useful words we can use to name things. First, we’ll see how to talk about one thing (singular: shyin, 'dog') and more than one thing (plural: shyin-yé, 'the dogs'). Also, we’ll see how we can talk about something specific (shyin-la ‘the dog’), and something non-specific (in shyin ‘a dog’). Some languages classify nouns by gender. Nouns in Kréyòl are like those in English, in the sense that they are are not typicallyclassified by gender. For some speakers of Kréyòl, though, nouns can be masculine or feminine. In this book, we’ve decided not to include these forms. It introduces a lot of complications which are not necessary for beginning learners that this book is hoping to help, since you will still be speaking great Kréyòl without including these features. Also, not all speakers of Kréyòl do classify nouns by gender. It’s good to be aware of it, though, since you may hear it when listening to other speakers of Kréyòl.

Here, as with everywhere in this book, you will see that there are a great deal of different ways of expressing the same sort of thing. For example, the word ‘languages’ might be translated as langaj, langaj-yé or lê langaj. This variation is completely normal: language is dynamic and diverse. Kréyòl is a particularly beautiful example of this diversity. To do justice to the richness of the Kréyòl language, we have attempted to include as many different forms as possible. All of these are equally valid, and you should not worry about any one being ‘more correct’ than any other. In choosing which forms to use, we suggest you practice your Kréyòl as much as possible with people in your family, your community or online to a find a way of speaking which feels authentic.
Say we just want to talk about some dog, not a particular dog, just ‘a dog’. We say ‘a’ in Kréyòl by using the word in:
Some people say un, so you can write it this way too. Also, if in comes before a vowel, it changes to ènn:
There’s another way to mark a noun as non-specific, using nothing at all:
If you want to talk about a specific thing, ‘the dog’, mark it with -la.
Some people also use le, la before the noun.

ex: They have the right to speak.

blocks.p: What about a bunch of dogs? In English, we add -s: one dog, two dogs.
In Kréyòl, we can just use the noun on its own:
Context will tell us whether we’re talking about one or more of something:
If we want to specify that a noun is plural, we can add -yé to the end:
We can use -yé when we want to mark a specific plural noun:

ex: Çété tô frèr ki volé poul-yé? Non, çé té vwazin-yé.
‘Did your brother steal the chickens? No, it was the neighbors.’

blocks.p: Another way to mark a specific plural noun is by combining the specificity marker -la (see above) and the plural marker -yé to form -layé.

ex: ‘Did your brother steal the chickens? No, it was the neighbors.’

blocks.p: Another way to make a noun plural is to add lê just before it. If you use this, you can’t use -yé in addition.

ex: Kan to manj krébis, to sis lê tèt.
‘When I’m eating crawfish, I suck the heads’

blocks.p: If we want to talk about ‘some of’ something, we can use the word dê:
Finally, if we’re counting something, we can just add the number - there’s no need to use -yé or lê here.

ex: ‘We have five chickens, three pigs and one old rooster.’

blocks.p: Pronouns are words we use to talk about things without having to mention the noun over and over again.
The subject is the one doing the action, the ‘I’ in ‘I eat rice’.

ex: We like to dance, y’all don’t like that.

blocks.p: The object is the one the action is done to, the ‘me’ in ‘They like me’.

Another use for this form is to emphasize the subject of the sentence by adding it at the beginning or end. You’ll probably recognize the distinctive Louisiana flavor of these sentences in English, too:
Possessive pronouns show who something belongs to. When we write these pronouns, we use the circumflex (the little hat, ^).

Sometimes, you will also come across people using forms like mê, tê, sê (for plural nouns) and mâ, tâ, sâ (for feminine nouns). Whether or not you use these, your Kréyòl will still sound just fine - and we note them here just to make you aware they exist.
If the subject and the object of a verb are the same, we need to use what’s called a reflexive pronoun. This is like English ‘herself’, ‘myself’, etc.

Emphatic possessive pronouns emphasize whose thing we’re talking about, and are equivalent to saying something is ‘your own’ in English. You do this by adding -chin, -kin, -chènn or -kènn to the normal possessive pronoun.
They can also stand alone, like ‘hers’, ‘yours’ and ‘mine’ in English:

ex: Our family is big, y’all’s is small.

blocks.p: Adjectives describe nouns. In English, they usually come before a noun: ‘a big house’. In Kréyòl, some adjectives come before the noun, but most come after the noun.

There are a set group of adjectives that come before noun, just like English: in gran lamézon / a big house. Some of these adjectives are shown below. Remember this group of adjectives with the mnemonic: adjectives describing BANGS (beauty, age, newness, goodness, size) come before the noun.
Apart from the BANGS adjectives, the other adjectives all come after the noun they describe.
For how to form sentences like ‘I’m hungry’ or ‘My truck is red’, see Verbs.

If you want to compare something to something else, you need to use pli … ke to mean ‘more … than’. Sometimes you can also hear pli … pasé for ‘more … than’, and mwins … ke for ‘less than’. If you want to say something is equal to something else, you can say osi … ke for ‘as … as’.

ex: My daughter is taller than your daughter.

blocks.p: Verbs are among the most important words to learn in a new language. In Kréyòl Lalwizyan, verbs are not conjugated like they are in French. However, some verbs have more than one form that you will need to learn as well as which forms to use in what situations. First, let’s introduce the two main classes of verbs in Kréyòl Lalwizyan: one-stem verbs and two-stem verbs.
One-stem verbs, as the name suggests, have one invariable form: they never change. An example of a one-stem verb is bwa, ‘to drink.’ Here are some sentences using bwa:

ex: He drinks a cup of coffee every morning.
Yé té pe pa galopé akoz yé té bwa tro.
They couldn’t run because they’d drunk too much.
I’m not going to drink that milk.

blocks.p: As you can see, even though the three example sentences are all in different tenses (present, past, and future, respectively), the form of the verb bwa does not change.

Two-stem verbs, on the other hand, have two forms: a long form and a short form. Which form you use depends on the situation. A common two-stem verb is parlé, parl, ‘to speak.’ Whenever a two-stem verb is listed in this booklet, the long form will be listed first (parlé), followed by a comma and the short form (parl). Here are some sentences using parlé, parl:

ex: Kan li té malad li té pe pa parlé.
When he was sick, he couldn’t talk.

blocks.p: In the first example sentence, the short form parl is used. In the other two examples, the long form parlé is used. It must be noted that not every speaker agrees on which verbs are one-stem and which verbs are two-stem. For example, some speakers translate the verb ‘to work’ as a two-stem verb: travayé, travay. Other speakers translate this verb as a one-stem verb: travay. These differences are fairly easy to detect with a bit of practice. But let’s return to two-stem verbs. We will be discussing when to use each of these forms (the long one and the short one) in the following sections.

As we already noted, verbs in Kréyòl Lalwizyan are not conjugated like in French. Instead of conjugations, Kréyòl Lalwizyan uses special words placed in front of the verb to indicate things like verb tense. In this way it is similar to the way the future is formed in English:

I walk (present)
I will walk (future)

In this instance, the future is indicated by the addition of the pre-verbal marker ‘will’ in front of the main verb ‘walk.’ Kréyòl Lalwizyan uses pre-verbal markers to talk about the future, the conditional, the present progressive, the past progressive, and the anterior past. We will explain each of these forms in turn.

To form the future tense, we simply add a form of the verb ‘to go’ in front of the main verb of the sentence. This is similar to English sentences like ‘I’m going to learn Spanish.’ There are two verbs for ‘to go’ in Kréyòl Lalwizyan: alé/va and kouri. In addition, there is a variant of va that only occurs when expressing the future tense: a. The most common way to mark the future is to use either va or a, but some speakers will use the form alé in front of the main verb as well. Whatever form of the future marker you use, it is always followed by the long form of the main verb (if it’s a two-stem verb). Let’s look at a few examples of va/a:
And let’s look at a few examples using other forms to express the future:

ex: I’m not going to watch TV today.
They’re going to play with the kids.

blocks.p: When you want to say something ‘will be’ in the future, you use the special word sa by itself:

To express the conditional tense in Kréyòl Lalwizyan, we use the pre-verbal marker sé. As was the case with the future tense, the main verb following the marker will be in the long form if it is a two-stem verb. Here are some examples:

ex: Mo sé kouri èk twa si mo té gin asé tem.
I would go with you if I had enough time.
She should be able to do it.
We’d like three large red onions.

blocks.p: To express an ongoing action, we use the pre-verbal marker apé or its shortened form, ap. This corresponds to English sentences like ‘I’m eating an apple right now.’ If the main verb is a two-stem verb, we use the long form following apé/ap. Note that the pronouns frequently combine with this pre-verbal marker, so mo apé would become m’apé. Here are some example sentences:

ex: They’re watching the sky to see the sunset.

blocks.p: To express an action that was going on in the past, we use two pre-verbal markers. The second one is the same as in the present progressive, apé/ap. Before that word we add the marker té, but because the work after it starts in a vowel, the two words usually combine to become t’apé or t’ap. Here are some examples:

ex: Dad was working in the yard when I came.
I was sleeping while you were cooking supper.

blocks.p: As with the other tenses we have looked at so far, we use the long form of two-stem verbs in the past progressive.

The past anterior is used to talk about actions that were completed in the past prior to another past action. The pre-verbal marker used for the past anterior is té. As with other pre-verbal markers, té is followed by the long form of two-stem verbs. Here are some examples:

ex: To té parlé èk li avan to vini isit?
Did you talk to her before coming here?

blocks.p: To talk about an action in the simple past, you use the long form of two-stem verbs without any pre-verbal markers. So for instance, let’s compare the present and the simple past of the verb parlé-parl:
For one-stem verbs, you simply use the pronoun and the verb. This means that for one-stem verbs, a sentence in the present can look identical to a sentence in the simple past:
So how can we tell the difference? Context will usually make it clear. This is always the case with verbs that denote an action.

Stative verbs (verbs that indicate a state of being) function a little differently. For these verbs, such as olé / to want, kapab / to be able, bezwin / to need, gin / to have, etc., you always need to use té, even if it is in the simple past. Here are a few examples:

In addition to the pre-verbal markers that we have discussed, there are other verbs that can precede the main verb in a sentence. We have already seen some of them: olé ‘to want,’ bezwin ‘to need,’ etc. Just like with pre-verbal markers, auxiliary verbs require us to use the long form of two-stem verbs:

ex: I need to go to the grocery store.
Do you want to have dinner with me tonight?

blocks.p: There are also phrases that function like auxiliary verbs such as gin pou ‘to have to.’ Here is an example of how it is used:

The verb ‘to be’ in Kréyòl Lalwizyan is a bit irregular. In general, the language does not use ‘to be’ as often as we do in English. In sentences with a noun and an adjective, you do not need to use a form of ‘to be.’ Examples:
However, there are instances where you do need a form of ‘to be.’ If you are equating two nouns, it’s necessary to use çé. This form is also used when there is no other explicit subject:

When there is no explicit subject and you want to express an idea in the past, you need to combine çé with the anterior past marker, té. If you are equating two nouns in the past, you only need the marker té:
It is also possible to form emphatic sentences with çé in instances where it is not necessarily required:
Another form of the verb ‘to be’ is yê. This form is used in questions and in relative clauses. Here are a few examples:
A third form of the verb ‘to be’ is dèt. This form corresponds to the infinitive. It is used in commands and when it follows auxiliary verbs or pre-verbal markers. Here are some examples:

ex: Would you like to be the boss?
Li olé dèt in doktœr ékan li vini gran.
She wants to be a doctor when she grows up.

blocks.p: Finally, to use the verb ‘to be’ in the future, you can either combine va (future marker) and dèt (infinitive) or use the marker sa introduced under the section about the future tense:

In order to express commands in Kréyòl Lalwizyan, we generally use to short form of two-stem verbs; obviously one-stem verbs use their invariant form. There are some speakers who make a distinction between formal and informal commands. For these speakers, the short form of a two-stem verb is informal and the long stem is formal. Here are some examples:

ex: Speak Kréyòl when you talk to me.

blocks.p: In addition to affirmative/positive statements, it is important to know how to make negative statements. The most common negative particle in Kréyòl Lalwizyan is pa. Its position in a sentence depends partially on the tense of the sentence. If the sentence is in the present, pa will come after the verb:
In the simple past, pa comes before the verb. Remember to use the long stem if it is a two-stem verb:

It is also important to note that certain verbs (principally auxiliary verbs and stative verbs) always come after pa, even if they are in the present tense. These verbs are very frequent in the language, and it will only take a little practice to recognize which ones behave this way. Here are a few examples:
When there are pre-verbal markers in the sentence such as té, sé, or va/a, pa comes after the marker. The one exception, however, is apé/ap:

Other phrases you might encounter in negative sentences include pa aryin/nothing, pa pærsonn /no one, pa nil-plas/nowhere, etc. In these phrases, the placement of pa corresponds to the rules we mentioned above. The other part of the phrase follows the verb unless the sentence is in the present tense, in which case it follows pa. Here are a few examples:
One common negative word that does not require the use of pa, however, is jamin ‘never.’ It generally gets placed wherever pa would be placed. If the two words co-occur, jamin follows pa:
Multiple negative words/phrases can be combined in the same sentence:

ex: Mo pa jamé wa pærsonn apé kouri nil-plas.
I never saw anyone going anywhere.

blocks.p: Adverbs describe how an action is done. These words generally follow the main verb, but there is some flexibility concerning where an adverb appears in a sentence. Common adverbs and adverbial phrases involve time and place. Here are a few examples of adverbs and adverbial phrases in Kréyòl Lalwizyan:
Adverbs can also modify adjectives. In these instances, the adverb precedes whatever adjective it is modifying:

In Kréyòl Lalwizyan, like English, there is a set order of words in a sentence: subject-verb-object. Remember that pronouns take different forms depending on whether they are subject or object, like ‘I’ and ‘me’ in English.
In this section, we’ll look at some more complex kinds of sentences so you can put together everything you’ve learned so far.
There are a couple of different ways of turning a statement into a question. Just like English, you can raise your intonation at the end of a sentence, keeping the structure the same:
You can also use the question word èske at the start of the question. This is like ‘Do you…?’ in English.
If you’re asking who, what, when, where, why or how, the structure you use is similar to yes-no questions, but you have to add those wh-words.

ex: What kind of truck do you have?
What time do you want to meet?

blocks.p: If you ask a question with the verb ‘to be’, remember you need to use yê.

Sometimes, we want to use a whole sentence to describe a noun. This sentence-within-a-sentence is called a relative clause. An example from English is ‘The man, who I met yesterday’. Or: ‘The man I met yesterday’. Both of these structures are also possible in Kréyòl:
You can also modify a longer phrase with a relative clause and ki:

ex: I have a cousin who works in Texas.

blocks.p: Sometimes, we want to talk about the relative clause itself, as in ‘I like what you’re cooking’. In these cases we can use ça or ça ki.

ex: She ate what I cooked for her.
Piti gin pou fé ça yê paren di yé fé.
Kids have to do what their parents tell them to do.

blocks.p: Other times, we want to talk about where something is. For this, we can use the word éyou (you will also hear its variants aou, ou, ayou, etc.).

ex: The town where I was born and raised.
Li té pa kapab trouvé éyou li shyin té.
He couldn’t find where his dog was.
